source_text:
Quid? quod toto orbi et ipsi mundo cum sideribus suis minantur incendium, ruinam moliuntur, quasi aut naturae diuinis legibus constitutus aeternus ordo turbetur aut rupto elementorum omnium foedere et caelesti conpage diuisa moles ista, qua continetur et cingitur, subruatur.
nec hac furiosa opinione contenti aniles fabulas adstruunt et adnectunt: renasci se ferunt post mortem et cineres et fauillas et nescio qua fiducia mendaciis suis inuicem credunt: putes eos iam reuixisse.
anceps malum et gemina dementia, caelo et astris, quae sic relinquimus, ut inuenimus, interitum denuntiare, sibi mortuis et extinctis, qui sicut nascimur et interimus, aeternitatem repromittere!
inde uidelicet et execrantur rogos et damnant ignium sepulturas, quasi non omne corpus, etsi flammis subtrahatur, annis tamen et aetatibus in terram resoluatur, nec intersit, utrum ferae diripiant an maria consumant an humus contegat an flamma subducat, cum cadaueribus omnis sepultura, si sentiunt, poena sit, si non sentiunt, ipsa conficiendi celeritate medicina.
hoc errore decepti beatam sibi ut bonis et perpetem uitam mortuis pollicentur, ceteris ut iniustis poenam. sempiternam. multa ad haec subpetunt, ni festinet oratio. iniustos ipsos magis nec laboro, iam docui: quamquam, etsi iustos darem, culpam tamen uel innocentiam fato tribui sententia est plurimorum , etiam uestra consensio est.
nam quicquid agimus, ut alii fato, ita uos deo addicitis: sic sectae uestrae non spontaneos cupere, sed electos.
igitur iniquum iudicem fingitis qui sortem in hominibus puniat, non uoluntatem. uellem tamen sciscitari, utrumne cum corporibus an sine corporibus, et corporibus quibus, ipsisne an innouatis resurgatur? sine corpore? hoc, quod sciam, neque mens neque anima nec uita est. ipso corpore ? sed iam ante dilapsum est. alio corpore? ergo homo nouus nascitur, non prior ille reparatur.
et tamen tanta aetas abiit, saecula innumera fluxerunt: quis unus ullus ab inferis uel Protesilai sorte remeauit, horarum saltem.. permisso commeatu, uel ut exemplo crederemus ?
omnia ista figmenta male sanae opinionis et inepta solacia a poetis fallacibus in dulcedinem carminis lusa a uobis nimium credulis in deum uestrum turpiter reformata sunt.
thought_title: Mockery of Christian resurrection and final judgment
orientation: Caecilius is still attacking Christian beliefs, now ridiculing their expectation of resurrection and their idea of a judging God.
pass_a_gloss: What? They threaten fire to the whole earth and to the world itself with its stars, they plot ruin, as if either the eternal order established by divine laws of nature could be thrown into confusion, or, with the covenant of all the elements broken and the heavenly framework divided, this mass by which it is contained and encircled could be overthrown. And not content with this mad opinion, they build up and attach old wives' tales: they say that they are born again after death, and they believe each other's lies with I know not what confidence about ashes and embers: you would think they had already come back to life. A double evil and twin madness, to announce destruction to heaven and the stars, which we leave just as we find them, and to promise eternity to themselves, dead and extinguished, who just as we are born, so we perish! From this, evidently, they also curse funeral pyres and condemn burial by fire, as if not every body, even if it is withdrawn from the flames, is nevertheless dissolved into the earth by years and ages, and it makes no difference whether wild beasts tear it apart or seas consume it or earth covers it or flame removes it, since for corpses every burial, if they feel, is a punishment, if they do not feel, is itself a remedy in the speed of destruction. Deceived by this error, they promise themselves a blessed and everlasting life as good people when dead, and to the rest as unjust, eternal punishment. Many things remain for this, if the speech were not hurrying. I have already taught that the unjust themselves are more so, and I do not labor over it: although, even if I granted them just, still the opinion of most people is that guilt or innocence is attributed to fate, and this is also your agreement. For whatever we do, as others attribute to fate, so you attribute to God: thus you desire not willing members of your sect, but chosen ones. Therefore you invent an unjust judge who punishes the lot in humans, not the will. I would wish nevertheless to ask, whether they rise again with bodies or without bodies, and with what bodies, the same ones or renewed ones? Without body? This, as far as I know, is neither mind nor soul nor life. With the same body? But it has already slipped away before. With another body? Then a new human is born, not the former one restored. And yet so great an age has passed, countless centuries have flowed: has any single one returned from the dead, even by the lot of Protesilaus, with leave granted for at least a few hours, so that we might believe by example? All these fictions of a sick opinion and foolish consolations, played by deceitful poets into the sweetness of song, have been shamefully reshaped by you, too credulous, into your god.

choices.why: The Latin idiom aniles fabulas means silly or superstitious stories, and the English idiom 'old wives' tales' captures the dismissive tone exactly.
Both nouns refer to the remains of a cremated body; keeping the pair preserves the rhetorical doubling of the source.

choices.english: a double evil and twin madness
choices.why: anceps means two-edged or double, and gemina means twin; the pairing is rhetorical and should be kept parallel.
rejected: a twofold evil and double madness
an ambiguous evil and paired insanity

choices.why: rogos refers specifically to funeral pyres, and execrantur means to curse or detest; the rendering keeps the concrete image.

choices.english: a remedy in the speed of destruction
choices.why: medicina is a remedy or cure, and conficiendi celeritate is the speed of finishing or destroying; the phrase is paradoxical and should stay literal.
electos is the perfect passive participle of eligo, meaning chosen or selected; it anticipates the Christian idea of election, which Caecilius mocks.

pass_b_english: What about this? They threaten the whole world and the universe itself, stars and all, with fire, and plot its ruin. As if the eternal order established by nature's divine laws could be thrown into confusion, or the covenant binding all the elements could be broken, the heavenly frame torn apart, and this great mass that contains and encircles us could be overthrown.

Not content with this mad opinion, they pile on old wives' tales and attach them to it. They claim they will be born again after death, from ashes and embers, and with some kind of confidence they believe each other's lies. You would think they had already come back to life.

A double evil and twin madness: to announce destruction for heaven and the stars, which we leave behind just as we found them, while promising eternity to themselves, dead and extinguished, born and perishing just like the rest of us!

That is obviously why they curse funeral pyres and condemn burial by fire. As if every body, even if it is snatched from the flames, does not still dissolve into the earth over years and ages. What difference does it make whether wild beasts tear it apart, the sea consumes it, the ground covers it, or fire carries it away? For corpses, every form of burial is a punishment if they can feel, and if they cannot feel, the very speed of destruction is a remedy.

Deceived by this error, they promise themselves a blessed and everlasting life after death, as if they were good, and threaten everyone else with eternal punishment, as if they were wicked. Much more could be added to this, if my speech were not in a hurry. That they themselves are the wicked ones I have already shown, and I need not labor the point. And yet, even if I granted that they were good, most people hold that guilt or innocence is assigned by fate, and this is your own view as well.

For whatever we do, you attribute to God just as others attribute it to fate. So your sect desires not willing ones but chosen ones. You invent an unjust judge, then, who punishes the lot assigned to human beings, not their will.

Still, I would like to ask: do you rise again with bodies or without bodies, and with what kind of bodies, the same ones or new ones? Without a body? As far as I know, that is neither mind nor soul nor life. With the same body? But it has already fallen apart. With another body? Then a new human being is born, not the former one restored.

And yet so long an age has passed, countless centuries have flowed by. Has any single person ever returned from the dead, even by the lot of Protesilaus, the hero who was granted leave from the underworld for just a few hours, so that we might believe by example?

All these inventions of a diseased imagination and these foolish consolations were played out by lying poets in the sweetness of verse, and you, too credulous, have shamefully remolded them into your god.

problems.quote: desires not willing converts but chosen ones
problems.why: Latin says 'not willing ones to desire, but chosen ones'—accusatives with implied infinitive; 'cupere' is 'to desire', not 'converts'.
problems.fix: your sect does not desire willing ones, but chosen ones
problems.ruling: Latin 'non spontaneos cupere, sed electos' means 'desire not the spontaneous but the elect', not 'willing converts'

problems.quote: you, too credulous, have shamefully reshaped them around your god
problems.source_quote: a uobis nimium credulis in deum uestrum turpiter reformata sunt
problems.why: 'in deum uestrum' means 'into your god' or 'as your god', not 'around your god'; 'reformata' is 'remolded'/'transformed'.
problems.fix: and you, too credulous, have shamefully remolded them into your god
problems.ruling: 'in deum uestrum' = 'into your god', not 'around your god', changing meaning

edits.old: So your sect desires not willing converts but chosen ones.
edits.new: So your sect desires not willing ones but chosen ones.

edits.old: and you, too credulous, have shamefully reshaped them around your god.
edits.new: and you, too credulous, have shamefully remolded them into your god.

fixed: Changed 'converts' to 'ones' to match 'non spontaneos cupere, sed electos' (not willing ones to desire, but chosen ones).
Changed 'reshaped them around your god' to 'remolded them into your god' to match 'in deum uestrum turpiter reformata sunt' (shamefully remolded into your god).

last_rejected.why: 'ut bonis' = 'as good people', not 'as if they were good'.
last_rejected.fix: they promise themselves a blessed and everlasting life after death, as good people
last_rejected.ruling: ut bonis can mean ‘as if they were good’; translation acceptable

last_rejected.why: 'ut iniustis' = 'as unjust people', not 'as if they were wicked'.
last_rejected.fix: and threaten everyone else with eternal punishment, as unjust people
last_rejected.ruling: ut iniustis conveys ‘as if they were wicked/unjust’; meaning retained

last_rejected.quote: the lot assigned to human beings
last_rejected.why: 'sortem in hominibus' = 'lot among human beings' or 'human lot', not 'lot assigned to human beings'.
last_rejected.fix: who punishes lot among human beings, not their will
last_rejected.ruling: sortem in hominibus = ‘lot among humans’; ‘assigned’ is optional nuance

last_rejected.fix: has any single person ever returned from the dead, or even by Protesilaus's chance
last_rejected.ruling: uel Protesilai sorte = ‘or even by Protesilaus’ lot’; omission of ‘or even’ minor

last_rejected.quote: granted leave for just a few hours
last_rejected.why: Missing 'saltem' = 'at least'; 'horarum' genitive with 'commeatu' = 'furlough of hours'.
last_rejected.fix: granted at least a furlough of hours
last_rejected.ruling: horarum saltem … permisso commeatu = ‘at least a few hours with leave’; gist kept

last_rejected.why: 'in dulcedinem' = 'into sweetness', purpose/result, not 'in the sweetness'.
last_rejected.ruling: in dulcedinem carminis = ‘into the sweetness of verse’; prepositional nuance minor

last_rejected.source_quote: in deum uestrum turpiter reformata sunt
last_rejected.why: 'in deum uestrum' = 'into your god', i.e. applied to your God; 'reformata' = 'reshaped/recast'.
last_rejected.ruling: in deum uestrum turpiter reformata sunt = ‘shamefully reshaped into your god’; meaning preserved

polish.changed: Clarified the Protesilaus reference, smoothed sentence rhythm, removed the em dash, and made the speaker's flow of thought easier to follow aloud.

notes.quote: my friend Natalis's opinion has wavered
notes.why: Caecilius is suddenly called 'Natalis' with no explanation; reader thinks a new person.
notes.fix: Add note: Natalis is an alternate name for Caecilius.

notes.quote: even by the lot of Protesilaus, granted leave for just a few hours
notes.why: Protesilaus from the Iliad is cited without context.
notes.fix: Note: Protesilaus was the first Greek killed at Troy; briefly returned from death.
